The statutory use restriction (52 U.S.C. 30111(a)(4)) covers names and addresses of individual contributors used for solicitation or commercial purposes. The committee-to-candidate file (pas2) carries recipient committee names, not individual donors. The treasurer-name column in cm is personal data and must be dropped. No paid data is needed. verified.pit_detail: I could not confirm a point-in-time receipt or availability date for any row, so this defaults to false. Verified: the bulk files are current snapshots with amendments folded in (18% of corporate rows in 1980 are amended), there are no vintages, and the cm80 file itself was modified in 2012. ORG_TP (the corporate classification) and CONNECTED_ORG_NM therefore come from a later snapshot, though they are mostly static attributes. IMAGE_NUM is not a receipt date (falsified above). Inference: using the transaction date plus a 3-6 month lag is probably safe, since the deadlines are monthly, quarterly and pre-election. A once-a-year formation like Cooper et al. (end of October, using the prior cycle) makes the lag almost irrelevant. That makes the PIT risk low and fixable. What remains are late-filed or amended transactions that were not public at the time, plus the 2010 Citizens United regime shift. A second, more serious leak is survivorship-linked coverage from name matching (see mapping), which no lag fixes. There is also no shares-outstanding field in the panel to control size, although the original paper's effect weakens under size and value controls.
verified.mapping_detail: VERIFIED: the FEC files carry no ticker, CIK or CUSIP, so joining is by name only. The stock panel, per NOTE_KO and META_v3, holds 1,503 tickers whose symbols are the source's last symbols. It has no company names, and its own notes say symbols must not be used for decisions. I fetched the public crosswalk Johnbrick123/sp500-data crsp_permnos.csv and pre1996/membership.csv (HTTP 206, 3 KB range each; raw.githubusercontent robots.txt is 404). Their columns are only label, permno, start, end, with NO names, so the permnos give no free name route. This is exactly T19's closed condition (permno-to-ticker needs paid CRSP). The dead labels (scout count about 890) need manual or LLM naming from ticker plus delisting month, with no free ground truth to validate against. Coverage will differ between firms later delisted and the rest; current survivors can be matched from Wikipedia and Nasdaq Trader. That reproduces the dvol-type leak described in NOTE_KO. Not tested by me: Wikipedia and Nasdaq Trader HTTP codes (scout-reported only), and any academic dataset linking PACs to gvkey/permno (DIME, Cooper et al. replication files). The latter would only help if it were free and mapped to permno, which still leaves permno-to-panel-label at the dead-label names gap.
fatal_flaws: Expected strength is far below the bar. The scout's own conversion gives a full-CRSP rank IC of about .025-.035 and an S&P 500 IC of about .01-.025, against the >= .05 persistent requirement. Inside the S&P 500 almost every firm has a PAC, so the signal range shrinks.

Literature: I verified only the abstract (JF 2010, 65(2) 687-724, 1979-2004, a positive cross-sectional link that is strongest for home-state and House candidates). The quoted alphas are NOT verified by me, including the claim that the three-factor alpha is insignificant. If that claim is true, the effect is largely a size/value tilt, and the panel cannot control for it because it has no shares outstanding.

Mapping wall, same as T19: the join is by name only. The crosswalk has permnos but no names, so about 890 dead labels have no free name source. Name coverage will correlate with future survival, which is a look-ahead leak of the dvol type.
No point-in-time receipt date. The scout's IMAGE_NUM-as-scan-date idea is falsified (83% of image prefixes fall before the transaction date). A conservative lag is the only defence.
The signal is annual and slow: about 34 formation dates between 1980 and 2014, so there are few independent observations for a persistence test.
verified.test_plan: Cheapest decisive kill test, about 8-12 hours, which avoids the expensive dead-label naming. (1) Download pas2 and cm for the 1980-2014 cycles (18 cycles; each pas2 file is 4-12 MB, so fetch one at a time with a 10 s delay). Keep only ORG_TP C/W, drop the treasurer name, and drop rows with TRANSACTION_TP outside 24K or with MEMO_CD set. (2) Map PACs to panel labels only for the clean, verifiable subset: the roughly 334 Wikipedia-matched bare labels plus the largest dead firms whose names are unambiguous from the 1980s CONNECTED_ORG_NM (e.g. GE, Sears, AT&T, Westinghouse). Freeze a match list of at most 300 firms before looking at any returns, and record the match rate separately for labels later delisted and the rest. (3) Pre-register one signal, with N=1 plus one industry-neutral variant, so N=2: at the end of each October t, breadth = log(1 + number of distinct CAND_ID funded by the firm's PACs over the trailing 24 months of TRANSACTION_DT ending July 31 of t, a 3-month lag). Rank only among matched S&P 500 members at that date. (4) Compute the monthly Spearman IC against 1-month forward returns from November to October, 1981-2014, through the lab (universe sp500, PIT IDs). Report the mean IC, its t-statistic, and the sub-periods 1981-94, 1995-2004 and 2005-14. Gate: kill if the mean IC is below .03 or the sign flips in any sub-period. Advance to the costly full mapping (30-50 more hours) only if the mean IC is at least .05 with the same sign in all three sub-periods. The prior says the kill branch is about 95% likely.

scout.name: FEC corporate PAC breadth (how many federal candidates a firm's PAC funds)
scout.info_type: Which federal candidates a company's PAC gives money to, and how many, taken from mandatory FEC filings. The registry has no political-connection or political-spending signal.
scout.mechanism: Political-capital rents that the market prices slowly (Cooper, Gulen and Ovtchinnikov 2010): firms that fund more candidates, especially home-state and House candidates, later have higher abnormal returns and earnings growth. The authors read this as slow pricing of the policy benefits.
scout.data_source: FEC bulk files at https://www.fec.gov/files/bulk-downloads/<cycle>/cm<yy>.zip (committee master, with ORG_TP and CONNECTED_ORG_NM) and pas2<yy>.zip (committee-to-candidate contributions, with TRANSACTION_DT, RPT_TP and AMNDT_IND). Headers are at https://www.fec.gov/files/bulk-downloads/data_dictionaries/pas2_header_file.csv and cm_header_file.csv. These requests 302-redirect to an S3 bucket (cg-519a459a-...s3-us-gov-west-1.amazonaws.com).
scout.access_check: Verified 2026-11-04. robots.txt (www.fec.gov) has Crawl-delay 10 for *; the Disallows cover only /data/...?* query pages, so /files/bulk-downloads/ is allowed. HTTP 200 for cm80.zip (359 KB), cm00.zip, cm14.zip, pas280.zip (3.9 MB), pas290.zip (4.5 MB), pas200.zip (7.8 MB), pas214.zip (11.9 MB) and both header files. The data are US government public records, free with no key. Inspected in this session: pas280 has 132,147 rows, 52,117 of them from corporate PACs (ORG_TP C or W); transaction dates are 99.999% filled; AMNDT_IND is N 86,705 / A 45,292 / T 150. cm80 has 1,383 corporate PACs and cm00 has 1,847. In later files CONNECTED_ORG_NM is often blank (in cm14, the PACs of American Express, Allstate, Aflac, Amazon and AMD have it blank), so matching must also use CMTE_NM. With a crude token match, 235 of the 503 current S&P 500 names appear in cm14 corporate PAC names; this is a lower bound because many PACs are named after subsidiaries. The cm files also contain a treasurer-name column (personal data); it is not needed and should be dropped on load.
scout.coverage: Election cycles 1979-80 to 2013-14 and later, transaction-level and dated. The signal could be rebuilt monthly or quarterly, which covers about 35 years before 2015.
scout.pit_notes: The bulk files are current snapshots that already include amendments (34% of 1980 rows are flagged A); there are no filing vintages. Use the transaction date plus a conservative lag at least as long as the reporting deadline. From memory, not verified here: monthly filers report by the 20th of the next month, quarterly filers 15 days after quarter end, and year-end reports by Jan 31; a lag of at least 2-3 months is safe. IMAGE_NUM on paper filings appears to encode a YYMMDD scan date (e.g. 790313...); that could give a receipt-date proxy, but this is an inference I did not check. Committee-to-firm matching must use only names valid at the time. If survivors get named from the current Wikipedia list while dead firms get a weaker manual match, 'has PAC data' will correlate with future survival. That is the same kind of leak as the dvol leak in research/data/us_stocks/NOTE_KO.md, so match coverage must be checked separately for labels later delisted and for the rest. The panel has no shares outstanding, so the signal cannot be controlled for size, and PAC breadth is partly a size and regulated-industry tilt.
scout.key_mapping: Joining is by name only; the FEC carries no ticker, CIK or CUSIP. Steps: (1) Bare panel labels: 334 of 613 match the current Wikipedia S&P 500 table (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_S%26P_500_companies, robots allows /wiki/), which gives name, CIK and GICS. Others still listed get current names from the Nasdaq Trader symbol directory (https://www.nasdaqtrader.com/dynamic/SymDir/otherlisted.txt and nasdaqlisted.txt, both HTTP 200; robots.txt is 404). (2) The 890 dead labels (TICKER-YYYYMM) have no free historical name source. 879 of them do have a CRSP permno in the panel source repo's public crosswalk (pre1996/membership.csv and crsp_permnos.csv on raw.githubusercontent.com/Johnbrick123/sp500-data). Their names would need manual or LLM-assisted naming, checked against the label's delisting month and the PAC's last active cycle. That is about 1,100 or more labels to hand-check, and it is the main cost. The Wikipedia S&P change log, the only free name history, is no longer on the live page, and old revisions sit under /w/, which robots disallows. Without CRSP, a join to S&P 500 tickers is feasible but costly and error-prone.
scout.registry_check: With neutral wording ('FEC corporate PAC contributions firm'), idea_check says 'new axis candidate'; the nearest entries are T24, S20 and E01 at 1.3-1.6, with no keyword overlap. Wording that contains 'stock' or 'per' triggers lexical false matches to S01 (price-based selection) and S02 (the keyword 'per', meaning PER/P-E ratio). Neither applies: this is non-price, non-accounting information. It is not among the OAP 168 signals (S20) and not part of insider or 13F cloning (S09).
scout.literature: Cooper, Gulen and Ovtchinnikov (2010, JF 65(2) 687-724), sample 1979-2004, 819k contributions from 1,930 firms, matched to CRSP by hand. From the paper text: one SD more candidates supported means about 2.61%/yr higher abnormal return (t 5.11-5.22). The portfolio weighted by number of candidates has a four-factor alpha of 21 bp/month (about 2.4%/yr), CAPM alphas are 39-48 bp, and three-factor alphas are only 7-11 bp and not significant. The index is formed at end-October and returns run November to October. The paper reports no S&P 500-only or value-weighted test. Aggarwal, Meschke and Wang (2012) find a negative link for soft-money donors, so the sign depends on the measure.
scout.est_strength: Inference, not measured: 2.61%/yr per SD is about 0.22%/month per SD. Divided by a cross-sectional monthly return SD of about 6-8% for large caps, that is a rank IC near .025-.035 in the full CRSP universe, where non-contributors are mostly small firms. Inside the S&P 500 most firms contribute, so the signal's range shrinks. The three-factor alpha is insignificant and no size control is possible here. Expected S&P 500 IC is about .01-.025, below the .05 bar.
scout.risks: The effect may be mostly size, value and regulated-industry exposure (the three-factor alpha is not significant). Name matching for about 1,100 labels risks errors and survivorship-linked coverage. The construct is annual and slow (low turnover, but few independent observations). Contributions shifted after the 2010 Citizens United ruling, which falls inside the sample. Using full-sample standardisation instead of an expanding window would add look-ahead. This candidate probably fails the .05 bar; its value is mainly that it is genuinely new and has long, verified, free history.

In the non-artifact hits (E01, T22, T23, T28, S22), no registry entry mentions freight, shipping, Baltic, Kilian or IGREA. A grep of research/open_data, bt1, breakthrough and wx1 also found nothing (a project-wide grep timed out). T22/OD1 used World Bank copper/gold, Goyal-Welch oil (wtexas) and Philly Fed survey. The signal's rank correlation with copper is 0.18 and with oil 0.15, so it is not renamed T22 commodity information. The use case, rotating between sectors, is the E01 family, closed with reopen 'none'. The S22 reopen condition asks for new non-price information with persistent stock IC >= .05, and this candidate does not provide that (see strength). Verdict: a new information type, applied in an already-closed implementation family.

VERIFIED in my replication: the scout's '1-month lag' is actually the correct real-time alignment. The value for month m-2 is used to hold during month m, because month m-1 is published mid-month m. With that alignment I reproduce the scout's numbers exactly (+0.148, +0.198, +0.087). A version that peeks half a month ahead (month m-1 value) is WEAKER (+0.059, +0.120, +0.095). An effect that does not get stronger with fresher data is a red flag for an information-diffusion story; it looks more like a slow cycle state. INFERENCE: (1) The full-sample linear trend drops out of 3-month differences (it only adds a constant), so ranks are fine. (2) The index was built after the fact: route panel and CPI deflation chosen in 2008, with a formula change in 2019. Pre-2019 vintages differ and could not be checked. (3) Before 1985 the inputs came from Drewry freight-rate publications, which were paid; a real-time investor would have needed them. The information existed but was not free. verified.mapping_detail: VERIFIED: joining by date to French VW 17-industry portfolios works. The fixed sleeves are CYC = Mines, Steel, Machn, Chems, Trans and DEF = Food, Utils, Cnsum. Mapping to NDX is a trivial date join. INFERENCE / not tested: a live ETF version is imperfect. There is no SPDR for Trans or Mines (IYT from 2003, XME from 2006), XLE (oil) is not in the CYC sleeve, and XLB/XLI/XLP/XLU start only 1998-12. The S&P 500 stock-level mapping (assigning each member to an industry by its largest loading in a 252-day regression on French daily industry returns) was not built or tested. The panel has no SIC codes and CRSP is paid.
fatal_flaws: Cannot reach either project bar. Index timing: next-month rank correlation with the 17-industry market is +0.013 (1969-85), +0.127 (1986-99) and +0.089 (2000-14), and the scout's P(up | signal high) of .646 against a .624 base is far below the ~.70 raw hit G1 needs. Stock level: the general beta-times-shock version gives cross-industry IC of -0.019 (scout). With only a two-sleeve membership signal, the implied S&P 500 stock IC is about .01-.02 (inference), well below .05.

Strongest form is a long-only CYC/DEF switch, gross of costs (about 2.4 switches per year) at 1x: Sharpe 0.53/0.88/0.67 in 1974-85/1986-99/2000-14 and 0.76 for 1986-2014 (CAGR 15.9% vs 12.0% for a 50/50 mix and 11.3% for the market). That is below the Sharpe 1.1 stand-alone bar and nowhere near 30%/yr without leverage. No leveraged sector ETFs existed before 2015.
Implementation falls in closed families: E01 sector rotation (reopen: none) and S22 regime->baskets. Using it to fill s0.85 idle cash would be E03 (closed).

Fragile to specification: the 1-month change gives near zero (+0.048, -0.020, +0.117). The fresher, look-ahead alignment is weaker than the correct one. The effect decays after 2000 (+0.087, t about 1.2).
Vintage not verifiable: the 2019 formula change, the ex-post route panel, and pre-1985 inputs from paid Drewry data.

scout.name: Dry-bulk shipping activity (Kilian global real activity index) -> cyclical-vs-defensive sector tilt (index timing only as a weak secondary use)
scout.info_type: Physical demand for moving raw materials by sea. Dry-bulk freight rates are a non-equity, non-commodity-price market where short-run ship supply is nearly fixed, so rate changes show shifts in real industrial demand. No registry family uses shipping or freight data.
scout.mechanism: Freight rates move when demand for iron ore, coal and grain shipments changes, weeks to months before that demand appears in the reported sales and earnings of cyclical firms (materials, steel, machinery, chemicals, transport). If equity investors react slowly to news from a market they do not watch, a rise in shipping activity should predict cyclicals beating defensives over the next 1-3 months. Inference: it should predict the index level less, because index returns also carry rate and valuation shocks.
scout.data_source: Dallas Fed page https://www.dallasfed.org/research/igrea and file https://www.dallasfed.org/-/media/Documents/research/igrea/igrea.xlsx (Kilian 2009 index with the Kilian 2019 correction). FRED series IGREA is a copy. Industry vehicle: Ken French 17/49 industry portfolios at https://mba.tuck.dartmouth.edu/pages/faculty/ken.french/ftp/49_Industry_Portfolios_CSV.zip; the project already holds a local 17-industry copy at /mnt/project-files/research/data/ken_french/raw/mirror_a91quaini/17_Industry_Portfolios.CSV. Live implementation could use sector ETFs: XLB/XLI/XLE against XLP/XLU, from 1998-12.

scout.pit_notes: (1) The index was built after the fact (Kilian 2009, corrected in 2019 after Hamilton's critique). It did not exist in real time before about 2008, although the underlying freight rates were public then (BDI daily since 1985). (2) Values are 'percent deviations from trend' with the trend fitted on the full sample. Signals should therefore use changes (a 3-month difference only shifts by a constant under a linear trend) or ranks against an expanding window, never levels. (3) The 2019 correction changed values, so pre-2019 vintages differ. Wayback copies of Kilian's older update files might allow a vintage check (not tested). (4) Lag: current practice is about 15 days after month end, so the 1-month lag used in my probe matches. With a 2-month lag, the 1986-2014 three-month effect halves (.17 to .087), so timeliness matters.
scout.key_mapping: Joins by date only, not by firm. For testing, the trade is between French industry groups fixed before looking at results: CYC = Mines, Steel, Machn, Chems, Trans; DEF = Food, Utils, Cnsum. For S&P 500 stocks, the panel has no SIC codes. The project's permno link (/mnt/project-files/research/influence/results/link_permno_col.csv, 1,323 columns) does not give SIC without CRSP, which is paid. scout.name: Oil futures curve shape (curvature of the WTI futures return curve) as an NDX 3x/1x/cash filter
scout.info_type: How the shape of the crude oil futures curve changes (front vs middle vs back contract returns). The paper behind it reads this as a forecast of oil supply shocks. It is separate from the oil price level or change and from roll yield (carry), both of which are closed.
scout.mechanism: Inference (paper's story, not checked here): the curvature factor forecasts supply-side oil shocks. Those shocks hurt non-oil firms with a lag, while oil firms are hedged, so a rise in curvature should be followed by weaker non-oil equity returns. NDX is almost entirely non-oil, so the signal would cut 3x to 1x or cash after a curvature rise. A secondary use is a long-only rotation from NDX into energy (XLE from 1998, or Ken French Oil industry before that). Clean B already marked energy timing by the oil curve as a closed 'cross-market relation', so that variant is the weaker one.

Optional cross-check: heating oil EER_EPD2F_PE1_Y35NY_DPGd.xls and PE4. Saved copies trimmed to 2014: /tmp/claude-0/-home-user--/e60ac389-f078-575c-af9f-bad532fab64a/scratchpad/ni1/scout/om/eia/

With a 504-observation expanding-window threshold, signals start around 1987.
scout.pit_notes: Exchange settlements are fixed at 14:30 ET, before the equity close, and are not revised. Using t+1 is still safer, and execution is at t+2 anyway. Construction risks: (1) Contract 1 rolls about 3 business days before the 25th, so returns must be computed within the same contract on roll days (C2 at t-1 to C1 at t), otherwise roll jumps leak in as fake curvature. (2) The paper's curvature weights came from a full-sample (1983-2014) PCA of 6 contracts. EIA has only 4, so fixed weights must be pre-registered (for example r1 - 2*r2 + r3 over 21 days, or r2 - 2*r3 + r4) or re-estimated in an expanding window. (3) Publication look-ahead: the paper's sample is our development window and it was published in 2017, so a pass on 1986-2014 is not independent evidence.
scout.key_mapping: Date-keyed daily series. NYMEX and NYSE trading days almost coincide; forward-fill at most 1 day. For the sector variant: Ken French 49-industry 'Oil' vs non-oil portfolios (daily, already in research/data/ken_french) or XLE from 1998. The S&P 500 panel has no sector codes, so a stock-level version would need betas estimated from prices.
scout.registry_check: idea_check returned 'auto-reject' against T18 (score 7.0, matched the words futures and contango) and, for the sector variant, E01 (matched rotation). T18 covers equity-index futures basis and Treasury month-end futures demand, not commodity curve shape. E01 is price-momentum sector rotation. Real neighbours: E04 carry, plus Clean B's CLEAN_B_CARRY_C0, which closed 'oil backwardation -> hold USO, else T-bills' on a KMPV 2018 literature ceiling (monthly IC up to .060). That traded oil roll yield; this candidate uses curvature to time equities. T22 and WX1-M1 wb_oil already used the oil price and its changes. Verified redundancy (1986-2014, monthly, no equity returns used): 1-month return curvature has correlation .08 with the 1-month oil return, .00 with the 12-month oil return, -.03 with Baa-Aaa and .02 with VIX. It is the most orthogonal series found in this modality. The level slope log(C1/C4) is more redundant: correlation .47 with the 12-month oil return, and R2 .40 on the closed set (weekly, 1990-2014).
scout.est_strength: Literature (Chiang & Hughen): out-of-sample monthly R2 of 2.3%, a monthly correlation of about .15, probably inflated because the factor was chosen on the full sample. Guessed realistic value: correlation .10 to .15. Inference, normal approximation: being 3x only in the favourable half lifts the G1 hit rate from .555 to about .59-.60 raw. With about 350 independent months, SE is about .026, and with about 10 trials the deflated value is about .50, far below the .65 keep bar. As an AND-filter on s0.85's 3x days, the expected gain is at most about +1%p/yr. That is a guess, not measured.
scout.literature: Chiang & Hughen, 'Do oil futures prices predict stock returns?', J. Banking & Finance 79 (2017) 129-141. Sample March 1983 to December 2014, monthly, NYMEX WTI first 6 contracts from Datastream. A 1%/month rise in curvature predicts a 0.4%/month lower market return. Expanding-window out-of-sample R2 2.3%. The effect appears in non-oil industries and not in oil industries. Driesprong, Jacobsen & Maat, JFE 2008, 1973-2003: oil price changes predict stock returns negatively, mainly in non-oil stocks (oil price itself is closed). Kilian & Park, IER 2009, 1973-2006: supply vs demand oil shocks affect stocks differently. Negative evidence: Hong & Yogo ('Digging into commodities' / JFE 2012, sample to 2008) found the part of aggregate commodity basis orthogonal to other predictors does not predict stock or bond returns. Fernandez-Perez, Fuertes & Miffre (RoF, Datastream, paid) report long-horizon equity predictability from backwardation/contango portfolios. Post-2014 numbers were not looked up.
scout.risks: The effect is probably concentrated in a few supply episodes (1990 Gulf War, 2008), with 2 to 3 big drawdowns in 1986-2014. The 4 EIA contracts cannot replicate the 6-contract weights. Sign or effect may not carry over to NDX, which is tech-heavy and less oil-sensitive than the S&P. A monthly R2 of about 2% is far below the R2 of about 9% (correlation about .30) that WX1 found is needed for 30%/yr. The idea was chosen after publication, which is selection bias. The low autocorrelation (-.31 monthly) means frequent switching and cost drag.

Choi and Ko (2002), as cited there, report 25-day CARs of 6.04% for buys from the trade date, but that is not tradable after disclosure. US evidence, from memory: Lakonishok and Lee (2001, 1975-1995) find insider purchases predict returns mainly in small firms; Jeng, Metrick and Zeckhauser (2003, 1975-1996) find about 6%/yr abnormal return for purchase portfolios; Cohen, Malloy and Pomorski (2012, 1986-2007) find about 0.8%/month value-weighted long-short for 'opportunistic' trades. scout.literature: Ko, H.-J. (2009), 대한안전경영과학회지 11(4): Korea, 2006 sample (link: https://koreascience.kr/article/JAKO200919038649281.pdf). Choi and Ko (2002), cited there. Lakonishok and Lee (2001, RFS, 1975-1995). Jeng, Metrick and Zeckhauser (2003, REStat, 1975-1996). Cohen, Malloy and Pomorski (2012, JF, 1986-2007).

(3) Parsing cost: about 150-270k documents (inference), which is 8-14 days of the 20k/day API quota, across several form versions (2.7 to 3.1) and cp949 quirks. (4) The documents contain individuals' names: parse numbers only and never store names. (5) Some delisted firms have a blank stock_code. (6) Signal breadth is low, so a monthly top-5 is often filled by few or stale names.

verified.test_plan:
Cheapest decisive test, about 8-12 hours, mostly name matching.

(0) Pre-register: N=3 signals.
- log in-house LD-2 expenses (registrant == client)
- year-over-year change in that log
- a 'lobbies in-house' dummy

Fixed lags: period end + 75 days before 2008, + 60 days from 2008. Originals only; amendments dropped.

(1) Mapping gate first (2-4 hours, decisive on its own):
- Take the panel members alive at Mar 15 of 2000, 2005 and 2010.
- Try to attach a free historical company name from the live Wikipedia S&P 500 changes table (check robots first) plus current constituents.
- Kill the test if fewer than 85% of members get a name in any year, or if the coverage rate for later-dead firms is more than 10 points below that of survivors. That asymmetry would bias the test.

(2) For the matched names, query /api/v1/filings/?registrant_name=X&client_name=X (in-house filings only, 1-3 pages per firm). About 500-700 firms x 2 requests is roughly 1,000-1,400 requests at 4 s each, about 1.5 hours. Store no personal fields.

(3) Annual formation every Mar 15 and Sep 15 from 2000 to 2014. Compute the cross-sectional Spearman rank IC versus next 1-month and 12-month returns among point-in-time members, with non-lobbyers set to 0 for the dummy and the level signal.
- Also compute a crude industry control: rank within the 10 largest LDA issue-code clusters. This is not a size control; no size data exist.
- Gate: mean monthly IC of at least .05 for the best of the 3 signals, after a Bonferroni-style deflation for N=3, AND the same sign in 2000-07 and 2008-14, AND better than the 'lobbies' dummy alone.
- Otherwise close the axis. Expected outcome: close. Record the result in the registry with add.

lab use: no (LDA data are not in the panel).

Add a margin, for example availability at period end plus 2 months. Amendments and terminations appear as separate filing types, so take the first-filed version where possible. Amounts are reported rounded (from memory: to $20k before 2008 and $10k after). As with the PAC candidate, name matching must be done the same way for dead and surviving labels. The panel has no size variable, so 'intensity' (lobbying divided by size) cannot be built directly; raw dollars or changes in lobbying would have to stand in.

Client names vary widely: 'PFIZER' vs 'PFIZER INC', subsidiaries, and outside firms filing on a client's behalf. The client_id field is consistent within a registrant but not across registrants. No CIK or ticker is included. The free LobbyView database (lobbyview.org) is said to link clients to Compustat gvkey; its robots.txt allows all, but its download terms and fields render through JS and were not tested, and a gvkey still needs a key we do not have.

I could not verify the sample span or the magnitude because the MPRA working-paper PDF is disallowed by robots; from memory the sample is about 1998-2006. Hill, Kelly, Lockhart and Van Ness (2013, Financial Management) find lobbying is associated with higher firm value.
scout.est_strength: A guess: rank IC of about .01-.03 within the S&P 500. With 16 years of semiannual or quarterly updates, it would be hard to show persistence across sub-periods. No effect size was verified.
scout.risks: Short history (1999 on) gives little statistical power. Lobbying scales with firm size and regulated industries, and the panel has no size control. Posting dates are unreliable, so fixed lags are required. Name-matching errors are likely. The literature is thin and its sample ends around 2006. This probably fails the .05 bar.

Production cuts and earnings downgrades should follow, and for NDX the tech-hardware inventory cycle matters most. Jones-Tuzel tie inventory growth to the risk premium: inventory growth tends to be low when risk premia are high. Proposed rule: rising inventories-to-sales means cut exposure. Background fact, not fetched this session: the Conference Board counts the manufacturing and trade inventories-to-sales ratio as a LAGGING indicator. That argues against short-horizon predictive power.

scout.name: Scheduled earnings-announcement-month premium (attention buying before known report dates), S&P 500 long-only
scout.info_type: Each firm's own report calendar (which month it will announce, predicted from its announcement months 3 and 12 months earlier). This is event-schedule information, not price level or trend.
scout.mechanism: Attention flow at a known time. Small investors buy stocks with a scheduled announcement coming up, so prices rise into and around the report. Frazzini-Lamont tie the premium to the volume surge and to imputed small-investor buying. The schedule is known months ahead, so a decision at month-end t (executed t+2) is not constrained by the 2-day delay.

scout.est_strength: Guessed, from literature magnitudes. With a long-short spread of 0.6-0.75%/month, a monthly cross-sectional sd of about 7-8%, and on average about 30% of S&P 500 names announcing in a given month, rank IC is about 0.02-0.04. That is below the 0.05 bar and well below the 0.08 S20 reopen bar. A long-only basket is roughly market beta plus half the spread, so a standalone Sharpe near 1.1 is unlikely.
scout.literature: Frazzini and Lamont 2007 (NBER w13090): main sample 1972-2004, also back to 1927; long expected announcers / short non-announcers earns over 60 bp/month, substantial among large caps, linked to small-investor buying. Barber, De George, Lehavy and Trueman 2013 (JFE): 1991-2010; US regression premium 0.326%/month (3.91%/yr annualized), US calendar-time long-short 75.9 bp/month, strongest in small firms but present in large. scout.risks: The effect sits mostly in the days around the report, and monthly holding dilutes it. Announcer share is concentrated in Jan/Apr/Jul/Oct, so the signal partly acts as a fiscal-calendar or sector tilt (retailers report off-cycle). It overlaps with Heston-Sadka seasonality, which S20 already failed. Long-only captures only the long leg. Turnover is near 100%/month. Spike dating errors weaken the signal further. Most likely outcome: a stable but too-small IC (about 0.03).

scout.name: Technology-link momentum: returns of patent-overlap peers (Lee-Sun-Wang-Zhang) inside the S&P 500
scout.info_type: A non-price, non-industry network: which other S&P 500 firms share a firm's technology base, measured by patent CPC-class overlap over the past 5 years, used to weight those peers' latest returns.
scout.mechanism: Friction: limited attention and processing complexity. Analysts and investors are organized by SIC/GICS industry. News that hits a firm's technology neighbours in other industries (for example, firms that share G06T or H01L patents but sit in different sectors) reaches the focal price slowly. Lee et al. find the effect is stronger when attention is low and arbitrage is hard, which points to slow diffusion rather than risk. Use it long-only: each month, buy the top quintile of tech-peer-weighted past return among point-in-time S&P 500 members. A slow-diffusion friction leaves drift that lasts weeks to months, unlike price pressure that reverts within days. That is the only friction type that can survive a 2-day execution lag and a 0.3-0.6% round trip.
